prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida She arrived as near to virginal as girls got in those days—i.e., young, the requisite dewy cheek flushed at its own daring. He had hoped for a little more edge. But she held the newspaper rolled like a scepter, his advertisement turned up to prove she was there solely at his bidding—and yet the gold band, the photographs ... a mother, then. He placed her in the old garden chair, the same one he went to evenings when the first tug on the cord sent the bulb swinging like the lamps in the medic’s tent over the wounded, swaddled shapes that moaned each time the Screaming Meemies let loose, their calculated shrieks so far away he thought of crickets—while all around him matted gauze and ether pricked up an itch so bad he could hardly sketch each clean curve of tissue opening.I shut my eyes, walk straight to it. Nothing special but it’s there, wicker fraying under my calming fingers.

Keywords: After, IVAN, ALBRIGHT

outputs.L1:
**After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida***

She arrived as near to virginal as girls got in those days—i.e., young, the requisite dewy cheek flushed by its own daring. He had hoped for a little more edge. But she held the rolled newspaper like a scepter, his advertisement turned upward to prove she was there solely at his bidding—and yet the gold band, the photographs . . . a mother, then.

He placed her in the old garden chair, the same one he went to in the evenings, when the first tug on the cord sent the bulb swinging like the lamps in the medic’s tent above the wounded, swaddled shapes that moaned each time the Screaming Meemies let loose—their calculated shrieks so far away that he thought of crickets—while all around him, matted gauze and ether pricked up an itch so fierce he could hardly sketch each clean curve of opening tissue.

I shut my eyes and walk straight to it. Nothing special, but it’s there, wicker fraying beneath my calming fingers.
outputs.L2:
**After Ivan Albright’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida***

She came to him with as much innocence as a young woman of that era was likely to possess: youthful, her properly fresh complexion reddening at the boldness of what she was doing. He had wished she would have more bite. Still, she gripped the rolled newspaper like a royal staff, with his advertisement facing outward as evidence that she had answered only his summons. Yet there was the wedding ring, and the photographs … so she was a mother.

He seated her in the worn garden chair—the chair he himself sought out at night, when the first pull of its cord set the lightbulb swaying like those lamps in the medical tent above the bandaged bodies of the wounded. The bundled figures groaned whenever the Screaming Meemies began, though their deliberately terrifying cries came from so far off that they reminded him of crickets. Surrounded by tangled gauze and ether, he felt an itch so fierce that he could barely draw the smooth contours of each opening layer of flesh.

I close my eyes and go directly to the chair. It is ordinary, but unmistakably present, its wicker unraveling beneath the fingers I use to steady myself.
outputs.L3:
A young woman named Ida arrives at the artist’s studio in response to his advertisement. She brings the newspaper with her, as though to prove that she has come at his invitation. Her appearance is strikingly innocent, almost virginal. The artist, who had hoped for a model with more sharpness or daring, is initially disappointed. Yet the wedding band on Ida’s finger and the photographs she carries reveal a more complicated identity: she is a married woman and a mother.

The artist seats Ida in an old wicker garden chair, an ordinary piece of furniture that also belongs to his private life. During solitary evenings, he sits in the same chair himself. As the studio’s bare bulb swings overhead, the chair and its shifting light awaken memories of wartime service. He recalls sketching wounded soldiers inside a medical tent, surrounded by screams, bloodied gauze, and the heavy smell of ether. The quiet act of drawing Ida is therefore shadowed by scenes of pain and trauma from his past.

Later, another speaker approaches the same fraying wicker chair with closed eyes. Rather than focusing on its appearance, the speaker explores it through touch, feeling its worn surface and fragile weave. In this tactile encounter, the chair becomes more than a simple object: it serves as a link between different lives, memories, and periods of time. Despite its associations with loneliness and war, its familiar texture offers the later speaker a sense of stillness and calm.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the complicated relationship between artistic perception, aging, and traumatic memory by imagining the painter Ivan Albright evaluating a young mother as a possible model. Albright’s attention transforms her from an ordinary person into a subject whose body bears the marks of time, labor, and vulnerability. Although she is still young, the painter’s gaze seems to anticipate the physical changes that age will eventually produce. This reflects Albright’s artistic fascination with decay and with the ways flesh records experience. The act of looking is therefore not neutral: it is both creative and unsettling, exposing the distance between the woman’s everyday identity and the body the artist imagines placing on the canvas.

The studio chair deepens this tension. It is initially a practical object, part of the setting in which a model might pose, but it also recalls Albright’s wartime work as a medical illustrator. During the war, his sketches confronted injured and damaged bodies directly, requiring him to observe suffering with clinical precision. In the poem, the chair becomes a bridge between that past and the present moment. Its worn surface carries an association with the wounded people Albright once drew, so that the possibility of making new art cannot be separated from memories of bodily trauma.

The poem’s conclusion makes this connection physical through a tactile encounter with the chair. Touching its frayed material reveals that memory survives not only in images or thoughts but also in objects. The chair’s texture appears to retain traces of earlier suffering, turning an ordinary piece of furniture into an archive of violence and loss. Its deterioration parallels the aging and damaged bodies that occupy Albright’s art, suggesting that material things, like human flesh, bear the pressure of time.

By ending with touch rather than sight alone, the poem complicates the idea of artistic vision. Albright’s art emerges not simply from detached observation but from sustained contact with mortality and pain. The chair embodies the enduring physical presence of the past, showing how trauma can remain lodged in the most familiar objects. Artistic creation thus becomes an act of remembrance: the artist’s attention gives visible form to what time has worn down but has not erased.
outputs.L5:
### After Ivan Albright

After encountering the work of **Ivan Albright**, ordinary surfaces no longer seem simple. Skin, fabric, wood, and metal become dense landscapes marked by age and decay. The American painter’s meticulous style transformed physical deterioration into a meditation on time, mortality, and identity.

Albright is especially remembered for creating the corrupted portrait in the 1945 film *The Picture of Dorian Gray*. Yet his broader legacy lies in the unsettling beauty of his paintings. Long after Ivan Albright, artists continue to explore the body not as an ideal form, but as a record of experience—fragile, changing, and impossible to separate from time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short ekphrastic prose poem inspired by Ivan Albright’s painting *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*, imagining the encounter between the artist and his model and incorporating memories of his wartime medical sketches.
counterfactuals.output:
Ida sits before the mirror, hat tilted like a tired halo, her powder puff stalled above the country of her face. Albright watches the light worry every fold of skin into gold, violet, ash. He remembers the hospital in France: bandages flowering darkly, torn cheeks mapped in pencil, young men staring past him while his hand learned not to tremble.

“Must you paint all of it?” Ida asks.

He thinks of those beds, the white sheets, the souls still shining through ruined flesh. “All I can see,” he says.

Behind her, the room tarnishes—comb, bottle, table, air—everything ripening toward dust. Ida raises her chin. In the mirror, another woman briefly gathers: girl, bride, stranger, bone. Albright lifts his brush as gently as gauze.

Into the world came a soul called Ida, and for a little while, under his terrible mercy, nothing in her was allowed to disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental literary passage that begins with “After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida” and moves between third-person historical fiction and a first-person museum viewer’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*, she sits in a room where time has learned to peel.

Ida is not yet old. The year is 1929, or 1930, or every year in which a woman, undressing, discovers that the mirror has kept a second calendar. Her satin slip gathers at her waist. On the table: powder, pins, a comb crowded with vanished hair. Outside, Chicago shoulders its factories into the dawn. Men descend stairways toward furnaces; women shake rugs from windows; the elevated train passes like a verdict.

She has been told not to move.

I stand behind the museum rope and immediately move closer.

The guard looks up.

Ida’s room is greenish, bruised with violet and rust. Nothing rests on a single surface. Skin is mineral, cloth is weather, the wall is an illness spreading beautifully. I try to meet her eyes, but the painting keeps directing me toward her hands—those knotted witnesses—and toward the small mirror she holds without mercy.

In the painter’s studio, Albright mixes another color that has no ordinary name. Ida waits. Perhaps she is a hired model; perhaps she has come from the boardinghouse with rent folded in her shoe. He asks her to turn her shoulder toward the light.

“What light?” she says.

The painter does not answer. He is searching the body for its buried architecture: vein, fold, tendon, the blue dusk beneath the breast. The century wants smooth women printed on cigarette cards, women lacquered onto automobiles, women without pores or histories. He gives Ida history enough to crush the chair.

I dislike him for this.

Then I dislike myself for wanting her rescued from the paint.

If I say *grotesque*, whose fear am I naming? If I say *unflinching*, who is doing the flinching? The label tells me about technique, dates, dimensions. It does not say whether Ida laughed during the sittings. It does not say what she bought with the money. It does not say if that was her name.

She shifts when the painter looks away. Blood returns to her foot in needles. From the street comes the cry of a newsboy: banks, breadlines, a government promising that collapse is temporary. Ida has heard this word before. Temporary hunger. Temporary work. Temporary room. Temporary face.

Only the soul, apparently, gets a title.

I read the title again: *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida.*

Not *a woman*. Not *a body*. A soul. Yet the soul arrives burdened with ankles, shadows, loosened straps, a stomach made public. I feel my own posture harden in reply. I become conscious of every secret seam: the scar under my shirt, the tooth I avoid with cold water, the small betrayal of my knees.

For a moment, the glass gives back my reflection over hers.

We occupy the chair together.

In 1930, Ida rises at last. The painter may protest, but she is finished before the painting is. She pulls the slip over her shoulders. She pins up her hair. In this version—mine, because history has misplaced the receipt—she crosses the studio and examines the canvas.

“Is that what you see?” she asks.

He begins to explain pigment.

“No,” she says. “Is that what you see?”

The museum closes in fifteen minutes. A voice descends from the ceiling, calm and bodiless. Visitors drift toward the exit, carrying postcards, umbrellas, the fatigue of having looked at too much suffering arranged in frames.

I remain.

Ida remains.

Between us, nearly a century thick, the paint refuses to dry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, lyrical paragraph about Ivan Albright painting Ida, including her newspaper, wedding band, family photographs, an old wicker garden chair, and the artist’s memories of wounded soldiers and “Screaming Meemies.”
counterfactuals.output: Ivan Albright paints Ida as though time itself had settled into her skin: she sits in an old wicker garden chair, the day’s newspaper loosened across her lap, its columns already fading into yesterday, while her wedding band catches a dim, stubborn glint beside the family photographs gathered like small ancestral mirrors. Every crease of dress, paper, cane, and flesh seems to harbor a history, and behind the patient violence of his brush stir Albright’s memories of wounded soldiers—their bandages, ruined bodies, and sleepless faces—and the shriek of “Screaming Meemies” tearing the air apart. Yet Ida remains composed amid this inward bombardment, frail and monumental, her body made a weathered country where love, dread, endurance, and mortality lie crowded together, refusing to disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic vignette in a modernist stream-of-consciousness style based on *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*. Blend imagined biography, sensual visual detail, war trauma, and an abrupt shift into the observer’s present-tense voice.
counterfactuals.output:
Into the world there came a soul called Ida, though the world, busy with iron, smoke, and the numbering of boys, scarcely marked her arrival. A room above a butcher’s shop; rain stitching the window; her mother’s cry folded into the clatter of hooves. Ida: four letters entered in the family Bible between a death from fever and a death at sea.

Now she sits before the small, accusatory mirror.

The room ripens around her. Wallpaper sweats brown roses. The washbasin holds a dusk-colored film; combs lie among pins and bottles like implements from a surgeon’s tray. Her dress, loosened at the throat, has the bruised sheen of plums. Satin gathers over her body in sulks and folds. Beneath it, the flesh remembers every hand, every winter.

She had been pretty, they said. Meaning the face once obeyed light.

At nineteen she buttoned uniforms in a laundry where steam made ghosts of the women. At twenty-two she married a man whose photograph showed one stiff hand upon a chair. France altered him. He returned with mud beneath his dreams, waking to guns inside the walls, striking at the sheets as if they were wire. Sometimes he called her Mother. Sometimes he called her by the name of a town he would not describe. His left ear was a pale, puckered silence. Ida learned to enter rooms without sound.

There were evenings when he sat over soup and watched the grease make rainbows. Then the spoon would drop. His eyes would widen at something advancing through the table.

Don’t you hear it?

Only the clock, she said.

No. Underneath.

Years later, after influenza took the baby and drink took what remained of him, Ida found a bit of shell casing in his coat. She kept it in the powder box. Brass, greened at the rim; one end jagged as a bitten tooth. She would touch it before going out dancing, as though war were a saint whose relic might protect her from loneliness.

But tonight—or is it always tonight?—the dance is finished before it begins. Her shoes pinch under the chair. One stocking has collapsed around the ankle. On the vanity, a hand mirror catches no heaven, only a warped patch of cheek: pores like wells, violet seams, yellow islands, the red flare where powder fails. Her fingers, jeweled and swollen, climb toward her breast. They hesitate there, surprised by the heart’s persistence.

How indecently the body continues.

The mirror gives back a country after bombardment. Chin, throat, eyelids: terrain churned and cratered, yet lavish, almost fertile. Every fold shines. Every blemish flowers. The painter’s light does not forgive; worse, it adores. It crawls over her knuckles, enters the green hollows beside her nose, lingers in the oily rose of her lips. It makes a treasure of damage.

Ida thinks of the first silk dress she owned, blue as gas flame. Thinks of oranges arriving at Christmas in tissue paper. Thinks of a soldier asleep against her shoulder on a train, though she never knew his name. Thinks of the telegram boy removing his cap.

The room thickens. Time is not passing; it is accumulating—powder over sweat, varnish over rot, memory over bone.

And then I am here.

I stand before her now, in the clean electric hush of the gallery, my own face faintly hovering in the protective glass. Behind me, someone’s phone vibrates. Shoes whisper across polished wood. Ida does not look away. Her ruined colors enter my skin: green, violet, meat-red, gold. I want to call her grotesque and cannot. I want to call her brave and cannot. She sits with one hand at her breast, holding herself together or opening herself—there is no difference—and I feel my pulse answer beneath my shirt.

The war is over. The war is never over.

I lean closer.

In the dark mirror beside her, something moves.

It is me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine the backstory behind Albright’s portrait of Ida: she answers a newspaper advertisement to model, arrives appearing youthful but is revealed to be a mother, and sits in a fraying wicker chair that triggers the painter’s memories of working near a wartime medical tent. End with a first-person reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
The advertisement was brief enough to seem harmless:

**MODEL WANTED. AFTERNOONS. NO EXPERIENCE NECESSARY.**

Ida arrived with rain shining on her coat and a ribbon pinned neatly beneath her hat. From the doorway she appeared scarcely older than a girl. Her cheeks were bright from the cold, and she carried herself with the deliberate lightness of someone entering a room where she hoped to become, for a few hours, another person.

Albright led her upstairs to the studio. Dust softened the windows; bottles, brushes, and small mirrors crowded the tables. In the center stood a wicker chair whose arms had begun to split into pale fibers.

“You’ll sit there,” he said.

Ida removed her hat. As she did, a photograph slipped from her handbag and skated across the floor. Albright picked it up. Three children stood on a porch, arranged by height, squinting into the sun.

“My little ones,” she said.

The phrase altered her. Not her face exactly, but the air around it. The youthful stranger at the door became a mother who had risen before daylight, buttoned coats, divided bread, soothed fevers, and answered the advertisement because money was short. When she sat, she did not fold herself shyly into the chair. She settled with the tired authority of someone accustomed to being needed.

The wicker creaked beneath her.

That sound carried Albright backward. He remembered wartime work near a medical tent: canvas snapping in the wind, enamel basins, mud tracked under cots, the sharp odor of antiseptic failing to cover blood. Beside the tent had been a heap of broken chairs and baskets, their woven reeds darkened by rain. Wounded men waited inside while orderlies moved among them, and everywhere the body seemed to declare the same truth—that everything living was being worn away even as it struggled to remain whole.

He began to paint.

Ida’s ribbon became a small flare of color amid grays and bruised greens. The wicker chair grew more prominent, its frayed strands curling outward like exposed nerves. He painted the fine shadows beneath her eyes, the soft collapse at the corners of her mouth, the hands that had washed clothes and lifted children. Each mark seemed to make her older, yet also more present. The girl who had entered the studio did not disappear; she remained within the mother, just as the unbroken reed remained visible inside the unraveling chair.

During breaks Ida spoke of ordinary things. One child hated oatmeal. Another collected buttons. The youngest woke from dreams and called for her. Albright listened, then returned to the canvas, where ordinary life took on the gravity of survival.

At dusk she stood, put on her hat, and asked whether he had made her look beautiful.

He studied the painted face.

“I’ve tried to make you look true,” he said.

After she left, the empty chair gave one last settling groan.

I stood before the portrait and understood that I had not painted age, nor poverty, nor even Ida alone. I had painted what the medical tent first taught me: that flesh remembers every burden, that beauty is not spared by time, and that its deepest form may be the courage to remain visible while time does its work.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
